input.question: How much have humans changed over the last 100,000-300,000 years?
input.ground_truth: I too am interested in this question! From what I've read, there are small biological adaptations that have happened in the last several thousand years but nothing that might be readily noticeable? For example, because we as a species started domesticating animals for our benefit around 8,000 years ago, that triggered an artificial selection which has resulted in most humans being able to digest lactose as adults, though some are still lactose intolerant. That's my understanding anyway. What I'm most interested in knowing though is has our species stopped evolving on a macro level because of our ability to change our environmental conditions to suit our needs through technology, or has not enough time passed in evolutionary scales for it to make a difference anyway?

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How much have humans changed over the last 100,000-300,000 years?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big, big family tree that goes way, way back. So far back that your great-great-great... (a *lot* of greats!) grandparents lived a long, long time ago—like 100,000 to 300,000 years ago.

Back then, your super, super old ancestors looked a little bit like us, but not exactly the same. They were shorter, had bigger jaws, and their heads were shaped a bit differently. They didn’t have things like phones or cars, and they lived in small groups, hunting animals and gathering food from nature.

Over all those years, little by little, our bodies and brains changed. We got a bit taller. Our faces got smaller. Our brains got bigger and smarter. We learned how to talk better, make tools, build homes, and work together in bigger groups.

So, we changed a lot, but not all at once. It was like drawing a picture, but instead of using one big stroke, you used lots and lots of tiny ones. That’s how humans have changed over a long, long time!
